item.title: Mediators say Iran never requested strike pause Trump cited
item.description: Mediators involved in efforts to end the U.S.-Iran war told The Wall Street Journal that Iran has not requested a 10-day pause on strikes against its energy infrastructure, directly contradicting President Trump's claim that the extension was made "as per Iranian Government request." The mediators also said Tehran has yet to deliver a final response to a 15-point American peace proposal aimed at ending the conflict, now in its fourth week.

item.title: Mexico says 40,000 of 130,000 missing may be alive
item.description: President Claudia Sheinbaum on Friday presented a long-awaited government report on Mexico's disappearance crisis, revealing that 130,178 people remain listed as disappeared over the past two decades, while acknowledging that a poorly maintained national database riddled with gaps, duplications, and missing data has hampered search efforts for years.

item.title: US confirms killing of IRGC Navy chief Tangsiri in Bandar Abbas strike
item.description:
Israel announced on Thursday that its military killed Rear Admiral Alireza Tangsiri, commander of the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps Navy, in an overnight airstrike on the Iranian port city of Bandar Abbas. The strike also killed Behnam Rezaei, head of the IRGC Navy's intelligence directorate, according to the Israel Defense Forces.

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu confirmed the killing in a video statement. "We continue to forcefully strike the targets of the Iranian terrorist regime," Netanyahu said. "Last night, we eliminated the Commander of the IRGC Navy. This man had a great deal of blood on his hands; he was also the one who led the closure of the Strait of Hormuz." Defense Minister Israel Katz described the operation as a "precise and lethal operation" and warned remaining IRGC members: "The IDF will hunt you down and eliminate you one by one."

U.S. Central Command confirmed Tangsiri's death hours later. Admiral Brad Cooper, CENTCOM commander, called on those serving in the IRGC Navy to "abandon their post and return home to avoid further risk of unnecessary injury or death," according to Gulf News.

item.title: Saudi Arabia urges US to intensify military campaign against Iran
item.description:
Saudi Arabia has called on the United States to intensify its military campaign against Iran and is weighing whether to enter the conflict directly, according to a Saudi intelligence source who confirmed the kingdom's behind-the-scenes role in shaping the nearly month-long war.

The intelligence source, speaking to The Guardian, corroborated a New York Times report that Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman has urged President Donald Trump in a series of recent conversations not to wind down the US-Israeli military operation against Iran, framing it as a "historic opportunity" to reshape the Middle East. The crown prince has pressed Trump to target Iran's energy infrastructure and even advocated for ground operations, including a potential seizure of Kharg Island, the hub of Iran's oil exports.

item.title: Iran fires cluster munitions at Tel Aviv, killing one
item.description: A man in his 60s was killed and at least two others injured in the Tel Aviv metropolitan area late Friday night after Iran launched a cluster munition missile at central Israel, capping a day of dramatic escalation in the month-old war. The fatal strike came hours after Israel attacked two Iranian nuclear facilities for the first time in the conflict — and as at least 10 American service members were wounded in a separate Iranian missile attack on Prince Sultan Air Base in Saudi Arabia.

item.title: Trump demands Iran reopen Strait of Hormuz for peace deal
item.description:
President Donald Trump on Friday urged Iran to reopen the Strait of Hormuz as a condition for any peace deal — and in doing so, jokingly referred to the contested waterway as the "Strait of Trump."

"They have to open up the Strait of Trump — I mean Hormuz," Trump said at the Saudi-backed FII Priority Summit in Miami Beach. "Excuse me, I'm so sorry. Such a terrible mistake." He predicted the media would seize on the remark but added, "there's no accidents with me, not too many." Trump drew a parallel to his earlier executive order renaming the Gulf of Mexico as the "Gulf of America" shortly after returning to office.

item.title: Poland's Tusk warns of imminent escalation in Iran war
item.description:
Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk warned on Friday that the war in the Middle East could intensify in the coming days, citing intelligence shared by allied nations as the US-Israeli military campaign against Iran nears the one-month mark.

"I have reasons to believe, also based on information we've received from our allies, that stabilization is unlikely in the coming days. On the contrary, a new escalation may occur," Tusk told reporters, according to Reuters, as carried by The Times of Israel.

item.title: Medvedev warns nuclear conflict between Israel and Iran is now 'inevitable'
item.description: Dmitry Medvedev, Russia's deputy chairman of the Security Council, warned on Friday that the U.S.-led war against Iran has made a nuclear conflict between Israel and Iran "inevitable in some form," as Western intelligence reports indicate Moscow is nearing the completion of drone shipments to Tehran — marking the first known transfer of lethal Russian military aid to Iran since the war began.

item.title: US land mines found near Shiraz kill civilians in first such deployment in decades
item.description: Images circulating on social media show what weapons experts have identified as American-made anti-tank land mines scattered across a residential area near Shiraz in southern Iran, in what appears to be the first confirmed deployment of US mines in more than two decades. At least one civilian has been killed and several others wounded after handling the devices, which Iranian state media described as resembling canned food.

item.title: IRGC urges civilians to flee areas near US forces as Trump extends Hormuz deadline
item.description: Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps on Friday urged civilians across the Middle East to immediately evacuate areas near American military positions, issuing the warning as the month-old war between the United States, Israel, and Iran showed no signs of abating despite a new extension of President Trump's deadline for Tehran to reopen the Strait of Hormuz.

item.title: IAEA warns strikes near Iran’s Bushehr Plant risk radiological crisis
item.description:
The International Atomic Energy Agency sounded its most urgent alarm yet over the safety of Iran's Bushehr Nuclear Power Plant on Thursday, warning that damage to the operational facility "could result in a major radiological accident affecting a large area in Iran and beyond," as military strikes continue to land near the site during the ongoing US-Israeli campaign against Iran.

IAEA Director General Rafael Grossi posted the warning on X, reiterating his "deep concern" about repeated strikes near the plant — Iran's only operational nuclear power station, located on the Persian Gulf coast — and calling on all parties to exercise "maximum restraint". He stressed the importance of adhering to the IAEA's seven-pillar framework for ensuring nuclear safety during armed conflict.

item.title: G7 ministers press Iran to reopen Strait of Hormuz
item.description:
UK Foreign Secretary Yvette Cooper declared Thursday that Iran "cannot hold the global economy hostage" as she joined counterparts from the Group of Seven nations at the Abbaye des Vaux-de-Cernay outside Paris to address the escalating crisis in the Middle East.

Speaking ahead of the two-day gathering, Cooper called for "a swift resolution that reaches regional stability and security and opens the Strait of Hormuz," the vital maritime chokepoint through which roughly a fifth of the world's oil supply passed before Iran's effective blockade began in late February. The meeting, hosted by French Foreign Minister Jean-Noël Barrot under France's G7 presidency, also drew U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio, who arrived in France overnight and was expected to discuss Iran over lunch on Friday.

item.title: All-perovskite tandem solar cell hits 29.76% efficiency
item.description: A burst of recent breakthroughs is bringing perovskite solar cells closer to commercial viability, as research teams in Germany and China have independently developed strategies to boost both efficiency and resilience in these next-generation photovoltaic devices.

item.title: IAEA says no radiation risk after strikes hit Iranian nuclear sites
item.description: The International Atomic Energy Agency confirmed on Friday that strikes on several Iranian facilities, including the Khondab heavy water production plant and the Khuzestan Steel Factory, posed no radiation risk, even as the agency's chief warned that continued military activity near the Bushehr Nuclear Power Plant could trigger a catastrophic radiological accident.

item.title: ASU method maps protein motion in hours, not months
item.description:
Scientists at Arizona State University have developed a method to extract the slow, sweeping motions of proteins from short computer simulations, a breakthrough published on March 26 in Science Advances that could reshape how researchers design drugs, tackle cancer, and combat antibiotic resistance.

The technique, called frequency-selective anharmonic (FRESEAN) mode analysis, identifies low-frequency vibrations — the deep, slow rhythms that govern how a protein bends, twists, and shifts between functional shapes — without relying on the simplifying assumptions that limited previous approaches. "We resurrected a long-standing idea that conformational transitions in proteins are tied to low-frequency vibrations," said Associate Professor Matthias Heyden, who leads the research group in ASU's School of Molecular Sciences. "We developed a method to identify these vibrations through natural fluctuations caused by molecular collisions".

item.title: Leiden scientists 3D-print microrobots that swim without a brain
item.description: Researchers at Leiden University have built microscopic 3D-printed robots that can swim, navigate obstacles, and adapt to their surroundings — all without sensors, software, or any form of electronic brain. The findings, published in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences on March 26, represent a departure from conventional approaches to microrobotics, where machines typically rely on external control signals or onboard computation to function.

item.title: Japan's Kikai supervolcano is refilling with magma, study finds
item.description: The magma reservoir beneath Japan's Kikai caldera — the site of the largest volcanic eruption of the Holocene epoch — is actively refilling with fresh molten rock, according to new research published on March 27 in the journal Communications Earth & Environment. The findings offer the first detailed picture of how supervolcanoes recharge between catastrophic eruptions and could improve monitoring of similar systems worldwide, including Yellowstone and Toba.

item.title: Iran war wipes $11.5 trillion from global markets in one month
item.description: One month after the United States and Israel launched a joint military campaign against Iran on February 28, the conflict has wiped $11.5 trillion from global stock markets and sent energy prices surging, reshaping the economic outlook for much of the world.

item.title: Hormuz oil crisis intensifies global push for renewables
item.description: Nearly a month after Iran declared the Strait of Hormuz closed to commercial shipping, the worst global energy disruption in decades is intensifying calls from governments, international agencies, and industry groups to accelerate the transition to renewable energy.

item.title: Japan backs US deep sea mining push in new pact
item.description:
The United States and Japan have signed a memorandum of cooperation on deep sea mining, agreeing to share research and support each other's ventures into the emerging industry. The non-legally binding agreement, signed following a meeting between President Trump and Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi in Washington on March 19, was subsequently circulated at a semiannual session of the International Seabed Authority, where 170 nations have spent a decade trying to agree on rules for mining the ocean floor.

The partnership represents the first major international endorsement of recent U.S. efforts to pursue seabed mining, which Washington has advanced largely on its own since early 2025. Diplomats and officials working on seabed issues described the agreement as an extraordinary public show of support for the American push.
